title: Hadley v. Baxendale
summary: A carrier was not liable for the mill’s lost profits on the facts the court accepted because the exceptional consequences of delay had not been sufficiently communicated when the shipping contract was made.
notes:
The notes compare later approaches, including assumed responsibility, Restatement § 351, and Article 2. They question the opinion’s application to its own facts. Those distinctions should remain alongside the rule rather than be collapsed into a statement that every foreseeable loss is always recoverable.

The parties: the millers (Hadley) sent the shaft through Pickford & Co., the carrier firm of which Baxendale was managing partner, to Joyce & Co. in Greenwich to serve as the model for a new shaft, after being told that a shaft delivered before noon would reach Greenwich the next day (Hadley v. Baxendale, 9 Exch. 341, 156 Eng. Rep. 145 (1854)).

The two-branch rule as usually stated: recoverable damages are those arising naturally, according to the usual course of things, from the breach itself, or those that may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting as the probable result of a breach.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs operated a mill in Gloucester. The defendants were common carriers trading as Pickford & Company, engaged to transport the mill’s broken crankshaft to the engineers who would use it as a pattern for a replacement.
sections.Material Facts:
The mill stopped after its crankshaft broke. The millers arranged transport of the broken shaft to Greenwich so that a replacement could be made. Delivery was delayed, delaying the replacement and the mill’s reopening. The claimed loss included wages and profits during the additional shutdown.

There is a significant tension within the printed report: its initial factual narrative says the plaintiffs’ servant told the clerk that the mill had stopped and requested immediate shipment, while Alderson’s application treats the communicated facts as only that the item was a mill shaft and the senders were millers. His reasoning does not accept that the carrier knew continued operation depended entirely on this particular delivery. The editors quote a later opinion that reads this as rejection of the stronger evidence. Both versions must remain visible when evaluating the result.
sections.Procedural History: The carrier paid £25 into court. A jury awarded the millers another £25 after being left without a sufficiently definite rule for the consequential loss. The Court of Exchequer ordered a new trial in 1854 and explained the governing damages rule and its application to the evidence it accepted.
sections.Issue: Which losses caused by breach are sufficiently within the parties’ contemplation at the time of contracting to be recoverable?
sections.Holding: Recoverable damages include losses arising naturally in the ordinary course and losses reasonably contemplated by both parties as a probable consequence because relevant special circumstances were known. The mill’s lost profits could not be included on the accepted facts here; a new trial was required.
sections.Reasoning:
Knowing that the shipment contained a broken mill shaft did not necessarily tell the carrier that any delay would stop all production. The mill might have a spare shaft, or other defects might independently prevent its operation. A total shutdown therefore did not follow in the ordinary course from the limited circumstances treated as communicated.

Where special circumstances are communicated, the parties can contemplate the resulting risk and negotiate price or protective terms. Holding the carrier to an undisclosed exceptional loss would remove that opportunity. The court thus separated causation from the scope of compensable loss: its delay actually contributed to the shutdown, but that causal connection alone did not establish responsibility for all resulting profits. The relevant knowledge is assessed when the contract is made.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Hadley supplies the organizing distinction between ordinary and special consequential loss. It also illustrates why factual notice and the procedural treatment of that notice matter as much as the verbal rule.

topics.remedies: Limits compensation to losses sufficiently contemplated at formation.
topics.foreseeability: Separates ordinary consequences from special losses requiring relevant notice.
topics.risk-allocation: Explains why notice of extraordinary consequences matters to pricing and allocation of responsibility.
topics.foreseeability-damages: Hadley is the source of the contemplation-of-the-parties foreseeability limit on consequential damages.
